div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: [The chief apartment in the Medicean Villa at Careggi, built for Cosimo, “Pater Patriæ,” from the designs of Michelozzi, and the favourite retreat of Lorenzo de' Medici. Through an Italian window, which stands open, can be seen the city of Florence, three miles distant; the Cupola of the Duomo, the Campanile of Giotto, and the Tower of the Palazzo Pubblico, rising clearly into the air.]
Bartolommeo Scala, Pico della Mirandola, Luigi Pulci, Lorenzo Tornabuoni. Enter Pier Leoni (right).

lg.l: How is Lorenzo?
Gallantly in spirit,
But with a subtle sluggishness of blood
That foils medicaments. In other men,
When fever finds a lodgment, pulses bound,
And fire curvets through vein and artery.
But in Lorenzo's body it eschews
All customary channels, diving down
Through subterranean currents to the seat
Of sensitive existence. He is like
Those flowers which in the summer of their bloom
Are dying at the root.
Out in your fears!
How would you have our princely prodigy,
Who ne'er in health resembled mortal men,
Be like them in disease? He oversteps
All common rules. What you conceive decay,
Will prove fresh efflorescence. I will lay
My poems 'gainst your physic that he lives.
A generous wager; but he soon may need
Nor Muse nor medicine.
What says Lazaro?
My colleague of Ticino daily pours
Golconda down his throat.
The whole of Ind
Were not too precious to save such a life.
To save it, yes! But lavish jewels are
As vain 'gainst death, within us, as without.
Death gulps no bribes.
The wolves were howling loud
All night above Fiesole, and gleams
Of intermittent light no fuel fed,
Flashed, ravaging the silence. Yesterday,
The caged Numidian lion rent his twin,
And roared for further havoc.
And did you hear
The midday lightning smote the cupola
Of Santa Reparata, toppling down
Masses of masonry, bricks, metal, tiles,
Towards the palace of the Medici;
While simultaneously a golden ball
Dropped from Lorenzo's scutcheon to the street.
Is it the first time wolves were heard to bark,
Stones seen to fall? Look! O'er the April sun
An April cloud comes flying. Shall I bid
Poliziano hug his amulet?
Be merry if you can. I would I were!
But, though you mock at portents, where is he
That likes to see the weather change for worse
About the hour of noon? Lorenzo now
Is in the just meridian of life,
When all man's various faculties should make
A marriage with each other; robust thews,
With a most delicate judgment; nimble brain,
With will impossible to move; a soul
To every air and motion sensitive,
Close wedded to a body, heat and cold,
Fatigue and indolence, and all the whims
Of outward circumstance unbudging leave
Alas! Lorenzo's immaterial part
From what he has substantial craves divorce.
O reconcile them quick, before the feud
Irreparable yawns. Should Florence lose
A mastery so mild, her course will be
Henceforth or sluggish or irregular.
His mind is like the rainbow, that bestrides
The earth with every colour, and hath rays
Beyond our seeing. Government with him
Is but a graver gaiety, while sport,
By him led on, takes princely dignity;
And like to Nature, whose device it is
To make a peace of all things, he includes
In his large self our petty contraries.
But look! he comes, with mildly lifted hand,
Accentuating wisdom to his son,
The young boy Cardinal.
And, Scala, see
The other arm familiarly flung
Over Politian's shoulder. Him he still
Loves best of all.

div.stage: [Enter Lorenzo, (left), with Poliziano, and his son Giovanni, a youth of seventeen, wearing the robes of a Cardinal.]

lg.l: Good morrow, gentlemen!
I was upon a fatherly discourse
To Giovanni, which I can defer
If you have pressing matter for my ear.
No, pray say on! Lo! Florence smiles below,
And in her streets moves jocund Carnival;
And whilst her mood is joyous, he who would
Another than Lorenzo's voice prefer,
Were folly's hopeless reprobate.
Well, next
Remember this. Be punctual as the sun,
Though others lag; for deference sits on youth
Better than any garment. Let your house
Be spacious more than splendid, and be books
And busts your most conspicuous furniture.
Buy gems for worth, not value. Of your sire
Imitate nothing save his sober love
For the chaste lap of learning. Feed your friends
With rare texts, not with banquets. Friendship craves
The commerce of the mind, not the exchange
Of emulous feasts that foster sycophants.
Select for intimates, if such survive,
Men like to Pico and Politian.
And not like Pulci?
Poet! be content
To have been loved by me. He will require
No wit save wisdom.
But if you should meet
Large spirits like to mountain streams let loose,
Twisting this way and that, as if to make
Life's journey longer and more various,
Treat them indulgently. Be not austere:
Outward austerity, as oft as not,
Is but the friar's serge 'neath which there lurks
More taste for sack than sackcloth. For the rest,
Remember you are mortgaged to the Church
Without redemption. Rome, not Florence, is
Henceforth your country. But if you be wise,
Yourself will be the undiscovered link
To couple them together. Where is Piero?
Playing pallone in the outer court.

sp.speaker: LORENZO.

lg.l: Playing pallone!

sp.stage: [Goes to the window, and gazes at Florence.]

lg.l: O, how fair she looks!
There never was a kingdom like to that,
And kingdoms have been played away ere this.
Pray for your brother.
So I do, that he
May lift his leading purposes aloft
As the sap rises.
Ah, they tell me, trees
Shoot only just as high as they dive deep;
And much I fear his shallow-rooted soul
Will soar but dwarfishly.
The Commonwealth
Hath made herself the sponsor for your debts,
As you for hers responded.
Welcome news!
Yes, I have been a spendthrift for the sake
Of my fair Florence, proud that she should wear
The splendour that hath beggared me.
So now
We must perpend what impost to prefer.
Well, have a care to tax men tenderly.
For if you pilfer all the eggs at once,
You'll find the nest deserted. Take but one,
To-morrow will another fill its place.
What news from Pisa?
News that doth not change.
Pisa still chafes against your government.
Then let the medicine, like the ill, not change.
'Tis fear unseats the horseman,—not the horse.
Touch his proud stomach with a rowelled heel,
He'll know a master rider.
Yet there comes
From Pisa, dear my master, such a gift
As in your eyes submission will outweigh.
Roscio of Pisa found and sends you this.

div.stage: [He points to a bust of Plato, which stands on a pedestal, and which he, Pico, Pulci, and Tornabuoni have been examining.]

lg.l: What! Plato's bust, in feature as he lived!
Pisa foro this must wear a looser chain.
How noble and familiar he looks
'Twixt Scipio and Faustina! The great gods
Are still at home in any company.
But how about the Pandects?
All but done;
And then unto the Codex. Martial's text
Prospers apace in Calderino's hands,
While Fontio tackles Persius.
All were well,
Could years revive like learning! I would fain
Make Florence wise even as she is fair.
But this activity we boast hath bounds,
And all the running waves of eager life
End on the motionless fixed strand of death.
Savonarola sermonises thus.
An easy way of preaching; you do well
To drag me upward from this drowning vein.
Half the reputed wisdom of the world
Is but the lack of sane sagacity
To lay the ghost of sorrow. But what news
Is current of the Prior of Saint Mark?
He makes a widening conquest of men's hearts,
And occupies them solely. Frà Mariano
Scatters in vain his honied homilies;
The flies have ta'en to vinegar.
A sour-souled monk! He came into my house,
And never asked for me. And when that I,
Not to be foiled in courtesy, repaired
Unto his convent garden, he, 'twould seem,
Was busy with his prayers. Gifts he disdains,
Confronting them as bribes, forgetting, though,
To send me back the library, the busts,
And all the antique fragments that my House
Have squandered on his thankless monastery.
Well, well, from Heaven when men credentials bring,
They often treat this poor earth scurvily!
I would have sent him long since to the Court
Whose arrogant ambassador he is.
What doth he here in Florence? You should raise
A wind about his ears to set his cowl
Towards Ferrara. Hard at prayers indeed!
His exhortations trespass on the State;
His sermons are sedition glibly faced
With a veneer of piety. He lights
The flame of disaffection in men's minds.
Beware, lest if you blow it out too hard,
You blow it in again.
Sir, I have sent
Valori, with four intimates, to mind
This pulpit-politician of the laws.
Have I exceeded my authority?
A seasonable message ne'er is ill.
But, for your choice, Valori is a vane
For every wind to play its whimsy with;
And the slim arrows of his wit will veer
Under the friar's gusty arguments.
Besides, I have suspected latterly,
Valori is indifferently drawn
Towards your rule, since you forbade him mate
With the lone orphan the Donati left,
The dainty Candida, who lulls her grief,
They tell me, with the mortuary drone
Of Frà Girolamo.
How comes she, in sooth,
To be so dainty? For a sorrier pair
Than sire and mother alike, I never drugged.
Is then your science, doctor, left at fault?
Know, Nature, like the cuckoo, laughs at law,
Placing her eggs in whatso nest she will;
And when at callow-time you think to find
The sparrow's stationary chirp, lo! bursts
Voyaging voice to glorify the spring.
Softer she be, the harder sure it seems
For him that must forego her.
Wherefore hard?
Why, look but on the first hedge-rose you meet;
'Tis lovelier much than any maid alive,
And is far more encased in innocence.
Its breath is sweeter, and if it should fade,
Well, you may pluck another. But a maid,
That you have once dissevered from her stem,
Upon your breast for ever must you keep,
Though all the scent of love evaporate,
And leave you but the stalk of what she was.
Is then this Candida so wondrous fair?
Fair as the world when yet 'tis hardly Spring,
But swelling buds and purpling coppices
Admonish it is coming.
There, replied
The close-observant lover! Happy you
Lorenzo Tornabuoni! for none else
Shall wear this vernal blossom on his breast,
Till moist Spring wax to Summer's parching heat,
To Autumn's too material fruitfulness,
Then wintry disillusion.
Back you glide
Into your sombre vein, traducing thus
The hues of life.
Life's a chameleon,
Whose colour is fit argument for fools.
But let us all to Florence, and defeat
These monkish menaces with merry songs,
Minted to mark the reign of Carnival.

div.stage: [Suddenly he totters, and stretches out his arm. Cardinal Giovanni and Poliziano are swiftly at his side, and Leoni approaches.]

lg.l: Feel you amiss?

div.stage: [Lorenzo recovers, and puts them gently aside.]

lg.l: No, nothing. There! 'Tis gone!
“Flower of the clove!”—How, Pulci, goes the strain?
Hence! hence! Come, Pico! Come, Politian!
Learning must now join hands with levity,
And foot a jocund round. We all must go,
Yes, you as well, my solemn Chancellor,—
All, saving Giovanni. Cardinal,
Keep gravity engaged till we return.
We shall be back to Vespers.

div.stage: [They all prepare to leave.]

lg.l: Fare you well!
And I will go refresh myself with work,
From the fatigue of too much idleness.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Piazza of the Duomo; the façade, and the Campanile of Giotto, at the Back of the stage.

[Enter a Carnival Procession of both sexes, the most conspicuous figures among which are Doffo Spini, Annibale Soderini, and Francesco Cei (right). All are running and romping. Some are masked, others not, but all are richly or fantastically attired. Many carry baskets of flowers, with which they pelt each other and the passers-by.]

lg.l: Now let us sing the song Lorenzo made
The year his daughter Maddalena wed
The Holy Father's son, Francesco Cibo.
Hush! Holy Fathers have no children, boy;
You mean his nephew.
Have it as you will.
Are we not all his children? Now, the song!
Not a new gown to honour Carnival!
When not the basest citizen but pours
His purse upon the pavement for his wife.
Mine is already empty. Look at it!

div.stage: [He draws his leathern pouch from his girdle.]

lg.l: Then why not swift replenish it? Your hands
Hang idle, while Lorenzo stretches his,
Imploring you for statues, miniatures,
Busts, anything you will.
And do you think
I, for Lorenzo, will my art demean
To make him more magnificent?
Others do,
And all their wives walk finely.
Fie on you!
What would you say, were I to bid you hire
Your beauty out to use, and urge you to it
By argument from others? Sooth, your gown
Is well enough
And am I beautiful?

div.stage: [She approaches and caresses him.]

lg.l: How you have caught the blackbird's homely pipe,
Now sweet, now scolding!
Better mate, I ween,
Than is the lark that only sings in Heaven.
Make thyself Heaven, and I will sing to thee.
Ah! to do that, I needs must go far off,
Or thou wilt ne'er think me celestial.
Then go and trim our nest upon the ground:
I am not always singing. But before
You homeward wend, this wisdom in your ear
Why do you come betwixt my Art and me?
In that, you are as foolish as the Earth,
When it thrusts in between the sun and moon,
And gets the light of neither. This eclipse
Bars me from art, and leaves you solitary.
Pass, and let each in turn illuminate
Your giddy round. Well, you shall have the gown.
Choose it as much like me as possible,
Who now am but a remnant, going cheap.
Dearer to me than any younger piece,
My gifted artist! Hark! Again they come,
The gaudy revellers. I straight will hie
And make my beauty yet more beautiful.
Ho! pretty maiden, will you sit to me?
To you, good sculptor! She's my model now.
How! When for marble did you quit the Muse?
I thought you were a poet.
So he is,
And I am sworn to marry him. His song
Hath made love liquid; he melts pearls of speech
I' the bubbling wine of a young maiden's blood.
Nay, marry not a poet. He will have
As many changeling mistresses as moods.
He wantons with the February winds,
And toys with March's forward daffodils.
He is an April fool each cuckoo-call
Can set a-gaping, and he falls in love
With every lamb that frisks its pretty tail.
He may love all, so that he loves me too.
Who would monopolise a poet's heart,
Large as the universe? It is enough
To sit within it.
May you never find
Its vastness cold. But, meanwhile, warm yourself.
Heed him not, sweet! the wisdom of the world
Is far too general; we poets are
Diverse as our detractors.
Be it so!
We women, when we love, are all alike.
Go like the sea and like the sea return,
Thou still wilt find me here. I am thy shore,
That slopes towards thee, and knows no other bent.
Nor will I ask if any fickle moon,
Swaying thee hither and thither, thy motions rule.
Smile on her as thou wilt and she on thee;
But thou must never so unfaithful prove
As to withhold the burden of thy moan,
When nights are dark and heaven untenanted,
From my deep-anchored lap.
I'll never leave it,
Though every star in heaven should shine on me.

div.stage: [Re-enter Carnival Procession (left), singing, dancing, and joking. Bettuccio and Letizia stand aside, hand in hand. At the same moment Savonarola appears on the steps of the Duomo, accompanied by Frà Domenico, Frà Silvestro, and other monks.]

lg.l: What do you here, you Pagan roysterers,
Roaring around the pillars of God's House
Your lewd fantastic canticles! The Sword
Hangs by a thread and is about to fall,—
To fall, ay, and on Florence. Put off quick
Your carnal garments, and make haste to don
The sackcloth of repentance, triflers all,
That, Christians called, are worse than infidel,
Blasphemers, usurers, slaves to fleshy lusts,
Mortgaged to Hell, whom Christ would fain redeem.
Blessëd are they that weep! You only laugh.
Shameless as Sodom are ye, and as deaf,
Seeing no star in the East! Accursëd be
Your obscene songs and foul frivolities!
Accursëd they that writ and they that sing,
Accursëd in their offspring and their doom!
The Sword of the Lord is sharpened, and your necks
Shall feel the smiting of its edge. How long,
How long shall I implore you, Florentines!
My voice is hoarse with calling, and my tongue
Cleaves to my mouth, and none is there that hears.
Look! in resplendent trim Valori comes,
With Bonsi and Vespucci in his train,
Luca Corsini likewise hurrying up.
We shall see sport directly.

div.stage: [Enter Francesco Valori, Luca Corsini, Domenico Bonsi, and Guidantanio Vespucci. Savonarola turns towards them.]

lg.l: Likewise you,
Who should uphold the Commonwealth and be
The solid buttress of the State, are but
Lorenzo's sycophants.
Who blasphemes now?
Cheers for Lorenzo! Come, my lads and maids,
Convince this kill-joy friar that your lungs
Have not gone dry with singing canticles.
Long live Lorenzo the Magnificent!
Long live Lorenzo and the Medici!
You hear them, friar? They use plain arguments.
But I wish gentler messages have come,
Commissioned by Lorenzo to lament
You use him so distrustfully. Other sons
Of Dominick, when lifted to the rank
Of Prior of your Convent, homage paid
To him their benefactor; but you flout
His pious gifts, and fling them in his face.
You count them gifts, I reckon them as bribes,
And have rejected them accordingly;
And as to my election, that I owe
Not to Lorenzo, but to God alone,
And unto God I pay my fealty.
May that be all?
Your answer is as rough
As smooth was his remonstrance. We are charged,
If failing in our embassy, to warn,
Still in respectful language, there are laws
That give disturbers of the city's peace
But choice of exile or obedience.
Go tell Lorenzo that it is not I
But he that will be exiled; exiled too
Unto a land whose exiles ne'er return.
Before the unrising Judgment-Seat of God
I summon him, Lorenzo; after him,
Shortly, Pope Innocent; and swiftly then,
King Ferdinand of Naples; and this Three,
To God must answer for the swinish trough
That Italy doth wallow in. The cup
Of her abominations now is full,
Full unto overflowing. Tell him that.
You are ungracious, Frà Girolamo!
God is ungracious, when men spurn His grace.
But you, Valori, in whose heart I glance,
You will be left to serve a nobler work
Before you die.
And, Friar, what of us,
My sweetheart and myself? Not every day
One gets one's fortune prophesied for nought.
The fountains of felicity run dry
When youth's no more in season. I will keep
A girdle and a hair-shirt for you, boy;
You yet may need them. Meanwhile, hold her sweet,
And from her heart divert all bitterness.
Come, brothers Dominick and Silvester,
We'll to our Convent.

div.stage: [Exeunt (right) Corsini, Bonsi, and Vespucci. Savonarola and Monks retire into the Duomo. The Carnival revellers break out again into merriment. A girl throws a rope of flowers round Letizia.]

lg.l: A girdle for Letizia!
And behold
A hair-shirt for Bettuccio!

div.stage: [She tries to put a sack over his head.

lg.l: Peace, you romps!
And pray you tell us, sir, if to our sports
Lorenzo be not coming.
'Tis the hour
He should be from Careggi on his way,
With a most gallant company. His friends
Are at the gate by this.
Then let us hie
Unto San Gallo, there to welcome him,
Fast followed by yon other stream of joy
That flows this way.
On for San Gallo, on!

div.stage: [They all pass out (left). As they do so, a fresh Carnival Company, headed by Soderini, enters (right), teasing and chasing Candida, who seems scared, and rushes to Valori for protection.]

lg.l: My pretty bird, how fast your bosom beats!
So roughly you a fledgling should not chase.
We did not plan to hurt her. She's so shy,
And with her foolish fleeing tempts pursuit.
Forgive me, sir, for clinging to your arm;
But they were me importuning with words
I do not understand, but much mislike.
But oh! 'tis he!

div.stage: [She breaks away from Valori.]

lg.l: Yes, maiden, it is I;
Who would protect you with these living hands,
If death were your pursuer. But why leave
So swift the port where you a shelter found?
They mean no harm. It was a foolish scare.
My comrades, hence! Lorenzo else will miss
The welcome you intend him. This coy maid
Hath found a bold protector. Thus it is:
The timid creatures call aversion fear,
But danger which they love, security.

div.stage: [Exeunt Soderini and the revellers (left).

lg.l: How gracious Fate hath been to me to-day,
Driving your fears this way!
Not gracious more
Than unto me providing at my need
Such valid help. I thank you, and farewell.
The hunted hare stops longer in her seat
When the tormenting greyhounds have swept by,
And found another scent. Stay just awhile,
Until the trepidation of your heart
Subside to gentler rhythms.
So it has.
My heart again beats temperately now.
Alas! alas! too temperately far!
But as the snug earth thaws the wintry snow,
Thy very coldness keeps my love so warm
That it must surely end by melting thee,
And make those icy lids and frozen orbs
Windows and eaves of dripping tenderness.
O sir! I pray you do not talk of love.
My heart is in the grave, my hope in Heaven,
Where my dear parents have preceded me,
Taking life's summer with them.
Say not that!
Grief in young hearts is like the nightingale,
Whose note is almost sweeter than 'tis sad,
And stays but briefly. Then when he is gone,
The cuckoo calleth lustier than before,
Proclaiming loud his victory of joy.
So, sweet, sad maiden, will it be with you.
There's silent winter now, silent and bare:
I have gleaned happiness.
Let hopeful love
But drive its furrow through the fields of death,
There yet will wave a harvest; but, if not,
Lend me your desolation, and we twain
Will still be sad together.
You forget.
If I could more than filial fetters wear,
For other chains Lorenzo destines me.
You speak of love and liberty to one
Who lacks the second even as the first.
Can you give one, the other being denied?
In the old lore of love I am not skilled.
But hearts need not be erudite to know
If love be sweet, compulsion must be sour,
And other maidens say that love is sweet!
I have not tasted it. But hark! they come.

div.stage: [There is the sound of returning Carnival.]

lg.l: Nay, do not go! I will protect you still.
Or, ere you go, tell me that love is sweet.
Sweet as a rivulet one stays to hear,
Yet doth not know its meaning. Be my friend.
Friendship, 'tis said, is love without his wings,
And friendship, sir, is sweet enough for me.
But I would rather be your love than friend,
For see, it follows, I could fly to you.

div.stage: [Enter Carnival Procession (right), headed by Bettuccio, followed by Letizia; also Anita, in her new gown.]

lg.l: Why, stripling rhymester, back again so soon?
Ill news, ill news! Lorenzo hath not come.
But he must come. What think you of my gown?
You should have bought it black. Lorenzo's eye
Will never fall upon your finery.
They say he's dying.
Let us go and pray
That he may live.
Pray for the obstacle
Of all I yearn for!
Hush! Love should at least
Be silent in the corridors of death.
Farewell!
Farewell But this, to take away.
Though from my lips thou may'st remove thine ear,
Withal, as in some sea-suffusëd shell,
The ocean of my love shall murmur still.

div.stage: [Exit Candida (right). Enter (left) Frà Domenico and Frà Silvestro.]

lg.l: Go home! go home! Lorenzo's hour hath come!
Lorenzo, master of your revels when
Life sat upon his heart and waved his plume.
Now death hath mounted up behind, 'twere meet
You should suspend awhile your carnival.
But surely, friar, Lorenzo is not dead?
Not dead, but now so tightly clutched by death,
That he hath sent for Frà Girolamo
To loose his soul.
No use then in my gown.
I would that I had waited. I must go
And pray them change it for a funeral one.
Savonarola's prophecy hath quick
Marched to its issue.
Ay, and look you, child.
He prophesied about Bettuccio's fate.
And wove a hair-shirt for your wedding night!
Yes, and a girdle, but not one of love.
My friends! it were more seemly to depart,
Since this grave news looks true. Lorenzo dead
Would shame your revelry; and should he live,
He will remember with due thankfulness
You put on gravity in time of joy,
Because he was not joyous.
True! Very true!
'Tis just what we were going to say, ourselves.
So let us separate.
Then come, Letizia,
And we will be as glum and miserable
As love will let us.

div.stage: [They all prepare to depart. The scene shifts.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: [The same as in Scene I., at Careggi; but a curtain is drawn across the stage, cutting off the interior of the apartment. Enter (left) Pico della Mirandola and Luigi Pulci. At the same time enter (right) Leoni.]

lg.l: What news, physician?
News most ominous.
Lorenzo, not contented to be shriven
By his own confessor, Matteo Bossi,
Nor by Frà Mariano, hath besought
That Frà Girolamo will hither come,
And ere he journey to the other world,
Arrange his soul.
The Prior of Saint Mark's,
Savonarola!
Even he in sooth.
He will be here anon.
You stagger me.
But often so it is: the steadiest souls
Seem to lose equilibrium when they stand
Upon the narrow edge that doth divide
This life from the deep precipice of death.
I had not thought it.
Doth he suffer much?
He must, though his brave visage still belies
The stomach's agonies, to which the gout,
Routed from limbs, hath sulkily retired.
He gleans no comfort from our tepid baths
Nor Bono Avogradi's heliotrope.
Are we to lose him then? Alas! alas!
The loftiest leaves are blown away the first,
While lowlier foliage melancholy hangs
Through half the winter!

div.stage: [Poliziano appears from behind the curtain, and draws it back. Lorenzo is seen reclining on a couch at the back of the stage, near the window overlooking Florence.]

lg.l: Lorenzo craves his dear familiars
To come as near him as they are in thought.
Will you approach?
Come close, Mirandola!
I could not die contented save I had
With thy young aspect first refreshed myself.
Learning and loveliness in thee have paired,
And seeing thee once more, I take farewell
Of all I lived for.
You are ruddier now.
Dismiss death's far too early messenger,
And bid him come again at stroke of age:
Give him not audience yet.
Death hath no hours,
But makes his own appointments. Better so:
For, Pico, I am out of heart and breath,
And could not breast the hill of life again.
But what a height, my master, you have climbed!
And if the moment to descend have come,
Survey once more the conquered territory,
And die believing that no mountain soars
So loftily as that aspiring name
That you will leave behind.
Consoling thought!
But, O Politian! if our labours live,
It will but be as tablets on a tomb
For sake of those that they commemorate,
Our names no more than speaking monument
To tell the world where a great spirit lies;
And we shall borrow from dead Plato's dust
What pinch of immortality we keep.
To Plato generous, why be thus unjust
To his posterity? Lorenzo's age,
Poised on its own broad pinions, shall defy
The downward gusts of time, while weaker wings
Are whirled beneath the horizon. Tongues unborn
Shall lisp the sweet survival of your deeds,
As children practise with a father's name
To learn a larger utterance.
Spoken well,
And worthy of my poet. But this vein
Of forward-reaching vanity infects
Each generation, this one most of all.
Nought new is said, but only newly thought:
And these pretentious novelties wherein
The upstart age struts proudly, are but gems
Carefully carven by an older time,
Now furnished with fresh setting.
Hark how he talks!
Too equably for one that is to live.
Only when death over our shoulder leans
And guides our childish fingers through life's page,
Write we in such well-balanced characters.
I want you all to hold in tenderness
Hieronymo Donato, Barbaro,
And Paolo Cortese, for my sake.
You know how they have traversed land and sea
To help me bridge the present with the past,
And open out for penetrating minds
Unexplored lands of learning. See you too
That Giovanni Lascaris, whose freight
Of twice one hundred volumes, ransacked fresh
From cloisters of Mount Athos, hath been sucked
Down by the ignorant waves, doth not receive
Less than the promised guerdon had he brought
That argosy to shore.
It shall be done.
Myself will see to it.
Pulci, to you
I do commit my poesies that have
Enjoyed obscurity.
They quick shall greet
The light that waits for them.
No, Pulci, no!
Consume them utterly. I would recall
Much that is now on every Tuscan tongue,
If that were possible. Our Plato held
The Muse should sing but praises of the Gods
And hymns to virtue.
You on me put a far more murderous task
Than I have heart for.
Friendship orders you.
Hark to the thrush gurgling in yonder tree!
He hath inhaled the liquid air whilst flying,
And, now he chooses him another perch,
Gives it us back in notes intangible;
Which is the very music that we want,
Did we but know it. For your spoken song,
Too full of meaning, lacks significance.
Hark how again he sings celestially,
The very heaven of music meaningless!
He is a better poet than us all.

div.stage: [An attendant enters (left), and whispers to Pico, who is joined by the rest. They confer silently, while Lorenzo gazes out towards Florence.]

lg.l: Does your debate concern me, gentlemen?
The Prior of Saint Mark is now without.
Then let him come within. He is a guest
That I have need of. Go, divert yourselves.
With him I must hold dialogue of death
Before life's curtain falls.

div.stage: [They take tender leave of him. Exeunt (right).]

lg.l: My intimates!
The best men ever had, but helpless now
To hold me here or cheer me thitherward.
Of all the company of hearts that sit
Round our existence smiling, that not one
Should be told off to see us to the land,
The road of which we know not! That seems hard.
To be alone in the full glare of life
Lulls fear to sleep. But loneliness in death
Might make the most intrepid spirit take
Shadows for substance.

div.stage: [The door (left) opens, and Savonarola appears. He stands pausing in the doorway. Lorenzo motions to him to approach.]

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Savonarola. Lorenzo.

lg.l: Will you approach, good Prior? 'Tis not from lack
Of reverence for your habit, that I fail
To greet you more becomingly, but death
That glues my limbs.
No need to rise, Lorenzo.
Heaven lays no tax of courtly ceremony;
But, being far more exorbitant, it claims
Full payment of the substance from the soul.
Why have you sent for me?
To readjust,
Before I journey on, unbalanced wrongs
That gall my conscience.
Show me them!
Since that it seems Plato avails not now.
Philosophy, like any false ally,
Comes to man's aid when need is at the least,
To shrink away in true extremity.
But Virtue, unaffected friend, contrives
To pull us through, though all the fiends conspire
To wedge us in with evil.
I have made
Elsewhere confession of my homelier sins.
But those transgressions that have walked abroad
In all men's eyes, I have reserved for one
Who knows no private favour.
Then speak on!
Death is the looking-glass of life wherein
Each man may scan the aspect of his deeds.
How looks it now, Lorenzo, now that God
Holds that unflattering mirror to your soul?
'Tis hard on twenty years since, but still, still,
The cry of sacked Volterra haunts my ears.
And well it may, Lorenzo! Do you think
Thus to divide eternity? Twenty years
Have placed no second 'twixt your sin and you.
I know it, Prior; and poignantly confess
To you and Heaven the guilt was mostly mine.
Endorsing claims equivocal to glut
The yawning coffers of the State, I clutched
A shadowy right; the alum mines were won,
And now the gain lies leaden on my breast,
Though bade I not the slaughter.
Hold! We bid
Whatever buttresses our bold designs,
And are the architects of every wrong
Raised o'er the ruins of demolished right.
You cannot take before the throne of God
The quarry of your hunting; but the blood
Clings to your hands.
Seem they so very red?
So red, contrition cannot wash them white?
For there is other gore that soaks my skirt,
Spilt in usurious payment of the blow
Struck by the Pazzi at my life, but spilt
Not from vindictiveness but policy.
Will policy avail to change the score
Of the Recording Angel? Hell is full
Of politic expedients, condoned
By Earth, to double their offence 'fore Heaven.
God saved your life; you slew your enemies.
Yet will He pardon even as He saved,
So anguish in the balance lift up guilt.
Is your confession ended?
Alas! no.
Full many an orphan maiden hath been robbed
Of dowry guaranteed; and virtue, shorn
Of its substantial outwork, hath succumbed
To the besieger. This seems direst wrong—
And is the direst wrong. The body pushed
Out of this life precociously may find
A better tenement. But he that fouls
A virgin soul and leaves it to corrupt,
Would strain God's mercy to the snapping-point,
If it were not far-reaching as Himself.
You must amend this injury.
Show me how,
And quickly will I do it.
'Tis enough.
Let restitution be in full ordained;
And, if you live, each victim ferret out
And wed her to the cloister.
Doing this,
May I the Almighty Arbiter confront,
And reckon on indulgence?
Nought that is,
Mountain, nor sea, nor the vast atmosphere,
Nor even man's stupendous scope of sin,
Can get beyond the circumambient range
Of Divine mercy. But before my hands
May absolution shower upon your soul,
Three things there are first indispensable.
What may these be?
Firstly, that you should have
Faith in God's mercy, living faith and full.
And that I have; for if I had it not,
How ill-caparisoned were I to start
Upon this final journey!
Next, that you
Make reparation absolute, and lay
This as a prior legacy on your sons,
For lingering wrong to friend or enemy.
To this you pawn your soul?
My soul be bond,
And forfeit if I fail!
Lastly, Lorenzo,
But mainly this of all, you must restore
Her liberties to Florence.
Friar, hold!
You overstep your territory there,
And make a raid on my dominions.
Remember what is Cæsar's.
Do I fail?
Where did you get your empire? Who was it gave
The Medici on Florence that sly grip
Which you have tightened? Nay, invoke not God!
For he as Cæsar ne'er anointed you;
And, failing His anointment, show me then
The sanction of His people.
What I have,
They freely gave.
They were not free to give;
For you with splendour first corrupted them,
Drugging their love of virtue, that you might
Their love of freedom violate, and they
The detriment discern not.
I gave all,
All that I have, all I inherited,
To vivify this city, and to lift
Her diadem of glory high above
All cities, kingdoms, principalities,
Lavished the substance of my House on her,
Discriminating not which hers, which mine,
And die with empty coffers that enriched
The fame of Florence. Was it crime in me?
In face of heavenly ermine will I claim,
For that, exemption.
Pandars might as well
Plead the foul price they pay, as you invoke
The substance squandered on the Commonwealth,
Whose freedom you have ravished. Well you know
In Florence that the government of One
Was an abomination till your Line
Drew all the reins of rule into its hand,
And jingling trappings of subjection laid
Upon a pampered people. Glory! Fame!
Fame is but sound; conscience makes harmony;
And happy he who truthfully can say,
When the world's pagan plaudits cease, he hears
The sacred music of a virtuous heart.
Give Florence back her freedom!
She is free,
And of her freedom made me what I am,
And by that freedom will unmake my sons
If they run short of wisdom.
Then, enough!
And summon your attendants.
You have need
No more of me. But this, Lorenzo, mark!
What you refuse, that Florence swift will take,
When your magnificence shall lie entombed,
And God arraign you for the rights you filched,
But could not carry with you, nor bequeath.
Die, by my voice unshriven!

div.stage: [His friends crowd round him. Savonarola turns to depart, but pauses, and gazes at Lorenzo with a look of austere menace. Curtain falls.]

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: [The Piazza della Signoria: the main entrance to the Palazzo Pubblico at the back of the stage, and the Loggia de' Lanzi on the right.]
Spini, Soderini, Cei, Compagnacci.

lg.l: I tell you what, my comrades, you must work.
There's little to be earned by merriment,
Since great Lorenzo died.
Work! I'll not work:
It is a turnspit's task.
Faith! then you'll starve:
A leaner task than turning any spit.
Wait till the French King comes. I wager, then
There will be food for fooling.
Fools for food,
Will prove more like. Which of you has not heard
His infantry in fight not only fell
But slay their enemies?
Uncivil boors!
They will learn gentler ways in Tuscany.
They're mighty slow at learning, then. The blood
Shed at Rappallo was but Magra's stream
Compared to Arno's, with the torrents loosed
At Fivizzano.
Why, they're monsters!
Ay,
Monsters in stature, appetite, and lust.
They ravish first, and rifle afterwards.
Upon the hale they wreak their savagery,
Then fall on the unarmed. They covet blood,
But ransom more. Your jewels, caskets, gems,
Velvets, embroideries, satins, silks, brocades,
All to their gullet stands for provender.
They think the stones of Italy, if sucked,
Will yield them oil; so meagre is their land,
So fat is ours.
Neither do courteous wiles
Disarm their greed. When Blanche of Montferrat,
Wearing her costliest jewels, on behalf
Of Savoy's Prince, because a minor still,
Proffered a gracious welcome to their King,
He took the precious gewgaws from her neck,
And for ten thousand ducats pawned them straight.
I've got no jewels.
But you've got a neck;
And, failing necklaces, your neck will serve.
Zounds! that it will.
I know Rappallo well,
Perched on the lap of olive-crested gorge,
And safely smiling at the smiling sea,
Till these ferocious foragers of death,
With swords for sickles, reaped each standing life,
Ripe or unripe, then gleaned the hospitals
For further slaughter.
But what wants this king
In Italy at all?
Why, just what kings,
Since crowns first turned their heads, are wont to want,
A bigger stage to strut on. This one claims
The fief of Naples. Florence has to choose
Whether to show a front or lend a side.

sp.speaker: SPINI.

lg.l: Hither comes one, to tell us more of this,
Marcuccio Salviati, with his kin:
A Piagnone, but an honest man.
How doth the slip of such a sturdy stock
Come to be bent by Frà Girolamo?

sp.stage: [Enter Salviati (right), followed by a number of Piagnoni, all dressed soberly, but some of them, like himself, armed.]

lg.l: What news, Salviati, of the Commonwealth?
The latest, Piero hath betaken him,
With Gianfigliazzo and Giannozzo Pucci,
Unto Sarzana, to the French King's camp,
To sue for terms for Florence.
Sue for terms!
A pretty suitor; barbarous, uncouth,
His mother's son.
But half a Florentine:
Expert in midnight broils and secret loves
A hero at pallone, passing on
All serious business to his Chancellor,
Ser Bibbiena.
Who is there denies
He is not like Lorenzo? 'Twere in vain
You asked the duplicate of such a Prince.
But he's Lorenzo's son, a Medici,
And that's enough. Whom would you have to stand
At top of Florence?
Better none than he.
Our Frà Girolamo's a likelier man.
Savonarola! A Dominican!
A monk! A vagrant from another world!
The pulpit is his place.
A place from which,
Worse plague upon't! already he directs
The hearts of half of Florence.
And ere long
Will guide them all. Pico, Politian,
Each in the garb of Domenick expired,
By him absolved. Say, did he not foretell
That the French King would come, and in the face
Of reputable citizens predict
Death to Lorenzo and Pope Innocent,
And Ferdinand of Naples last of all?
And each is gone.
A holy prophecy!
That robs us of Lorenzo, and exalts
Roderigo Borgia to St. Peter's Chair,
Thanks to the mule-loads of ill-gotten gold
Into Ascanio Sforza's palace driven
At time of conclave.
That was not the work
Of Frà Girolamo. But yesterday
He thundered in the pulpit of Saint Mark
'Gainst the election simoniacal
Of the new Pontiff.
Whereby he invents
Fresh enemies for Florence. Pious work!
The enemies of Florence are within.
Who is there pleads like Frà Girolamo
For restitution of our ancient rights?
And we will have them.
Have them, that we will.
Down with the Medici!

div.stage: [Enter (left) Lorenzo Tornabuoni.]

lg.l: Down, down, yourselves,
You sniggering whimperers, hangers on the skirt
Of an officious shaveling! Clasp your palms,
And mumble litanies, or flog your flesh!
But dare to meddle with the Commonwealth,
There are who will convince you of your place.
Ay, that there are, and quickly.

div.stage: [The two parties, the Compagnacci and the Piagnoni, lay their hands on their swords, and assume an attitude of menace towards one another. Salviati, by gesture, seeks to calm the Piagnoni.]

lg.l: Heed them not,
Lascivious brawlers! Let us bear their jibes,
And prove our Christian humility.
So very humble: humble as your monk,
Who sets himself above the Signory,
And—

div.stage: [Enter Savonarola (left), accompanied by Frà Domenico and Frà Silvestro.]

lg.l: Brethren! Citizens! Why, what is this!
Is this a time for Pagan acrimony,
When round your city adversaries throng
Dense as lean wolves in wintry Apennine?
Have I not warned you that the Church, and not
The Church alone, but equally the State,
And most this State of Florence, will be scourged,
And renovated next, and that ere long?
Hear yet another vision. In the night
I saw a hand in Heaven, and in the hand
A sword upon whose steel was brightly chased,
“The Sword of the Lord over the earth, swiftly and soon!”
And many voices heard I, plain and clear,
Promising mercy to the good, but loud
Stripes and confusion menacing to the ill,
And clamouring that the wrath of God is nigh.
The air grew pitchy dark, and thickly rained
Swords, lightnings, spears, and fiery javelins.
Rumbled the thunder, and the whole earth lay
A prey to battle, famine, pestilence.
Then, ere the vision vanished, came a voice
Commanding me to frighten you with fear,
And prophesy fresh scourges. Hear again!
The Sword of the Lord over the earth, swiftly and soon!
'Tis imminent to fall, nor can you get
Beyond its smiting. O convert you quick,
Beseeching God to stay His ire and send
True pastors who may win back vagrant souls.
The sword of the Lord! the sword of the Lord! I say,
Swiftly and soon!
And who commissioned you
Such scourges to invoke? If Florence feels
The trembling of the air a sword divides,
Who bade the French King swoop down Apennine,
And hover o'er this city? You are leagued
With Ludovico il Moro to inflict
Upon us this invasion.
To foretell
Is not to fashion. I but prophesied;
And have not these my prophecies come true?
Lo! I will bring the waters over the Earth!
And over the Earth they are coming! Yet why fear?
Enter the Ark, all ye who will: its doors
Stand open still. Let all of you be quick,
For coming is the time they will be shut,
And who then stand outside the Ark of God,
Will smite their breasts in bootless penitence.
Yes! the New Cyrus comes, God's Scourge he comes,
And all who will repent not shall be scourged.
The prophecies are verified, the Sword
At length, at length is here! Over is the time,
Over, O Florence, the time for dance and song,
And in its stead hath come the time for tears.
Thy sins, O Florence! and thy sins, O Rome!
O Italy! thy sins, this scourge have caused.
How often have I clamoured in thy ears,
How often wept, O Florence, that my voice
Might yet suffice thee! Unto Thee, O Lord,
To Thee, to Thee who died for us, I turn!
Pardon the people of Florence who would fain,
Though tardily, be Thine!
And why should they
Be spared, and others spared not? You have lured
A curse to Italy, and now would waive
The mischief from our heads!
And he will do it.
Trust him, he will, and Florence will be spared.
Hush, man! He's going to prophesy again.
And who is man, to argue with his God?
Hath not the potter power upon the clay,
And of the self-same lump may he not make
That vessel to dishonour,—honour this?
Tell me, O Magdalen! why now you dwell
In Paradise, who sinned as even we?
Why, Peter, who on Tabor's Mount beheld
Your Lord transfigured, yet denied Him thrice
Shamefacedly to lowly handmaiden,
Why do you now beatitude possess,
And yours the headship of God's Church? Thy sins,
Thy many sins, are all forgiven thee,
Since thou from alabaster vase didst pour
Unguents, and on His feet repentant tears.
Not for thy merits, Magdalen! and not
For thine, O Florence, art thou privileged,
But that God loves and favours whom He will.
Pray, and give alms, or else the sword will fall!
Hence to Saint Mark's, to Vespers!

div.stage: [Savonarola, accompanied by Frà Domenico and Frà Silvestro, crosses the stage, the Compagnacci making way for them. Exeunt (right), followed by Salviati and the Piagnoni. Bertuccio meanwhile has entered, and remains behind with Tornabuoni, Spini, and the Compagnacci.]

lg.l: You see the drift he has upon their wills.
They speed along like leaves before the wind,
And only halt until he blows again.
More reason that our breath be timely spent
On things less volatile. Paolo Orsini
Hath left for Lucca, in obedience
To orders from Piero. In his place,
Keep an unwinking eye upon the Gates:
These Whimperers mean mischief. Hence at once;
And while they pray, do more effectual work.
Come, Soderini, Cei, comrades all,
We now have occupation.

div.stage: [Exeunt Spini and Compagnacci (left).]

lg.l: With your leave,
I too, sir, will depart.
Unto your love?
O happy swain, that like the shepherd's star
Are in the evening just as near the sun
As in the morning.
Prettily conceived:
But you wrong both with your comparisons
She is the star, and follows in my wake,
Although I be no sun. She shines afar
Of her own lovingness, and makes the dark
Glow like the noon, and distance feel as near
As though I touched it.
Ah! I plain can see
You see her plain, although I see her not.
Where is she now?
With me, in verity:
Ostensibly with Grosso, whose fine touch
Hath begged her for a model.
And you lent!
Lent willingly. 'Twere churlish to refuse.
Is she then such a model, round and round?
She hath no other merit save to love;
But this one virtue so transports her sex,
That all her faults are lifted from the ground,
And nothing foul can touch her.
Hath she wit?
Just enough wit for apprehending mine.
She is the sap and would not be the tree,
Moves like the leaf nor wants to be the wind:
Insensibly and passively she lends
Her motions to the instincts of assent,
And spends her freedom in obedience.
You spoke of stars. See you, 'tis not a chain
That makes them one same centre circle round,
But faithful parallels; they, but for these,
Would rush against each other or apart.
Still may to you all stars propitious be!
They love me not.
It is my low estate
Makes my security. Were I like you,
Noble, esteemed, conspicuous in men's eyes,
The coyest and most shrinking joy there is
Might fly me too. I'm a poor poet, sir!
Cheaply reputed, yet so dearly loved,
That if you thrust your rapier through the Earth
Till it protruded on the other side,
You would not fathom it; and so, farewell!
Prosper in your ambitions!
Stay, sweet youth;
For the ambition warmest in my blood
Is but to be as happy as you boast.
I love the Lady Candida, but she
Confronts me icily. Now the fair maid,
Who is your shadow, is her shadow too.
I mark them much together.
They are twin.
But have you never noted, when a maid
Is in the first strange flow and flush of love,
She oft will lavish on the passive form
Of some near maid the fond experiments
Her instinct is too maidenly to prove
On our responsive selves?
You poets mark
So many things in women that we miss.
But I would fain you said an honest word
To this your sweet, that she in turn would say
An honest word for me to—well, you know—
To her who is more sweet to me because
I yet have tasted but her bitterness.
I your ambassador will be with zeal.
But from Letizia latterly I heard
That, save for Frà Girolamo's assent,
This comely orphan would her tresses clip,
Frame her young forehead in a plaitless veil,
And at her girdle hang a rosary.
Is it she may the better fly from me?
Vex not yourself. Whatever maids affect,
Tends but one way. Clasp they a crucifix,
'Tis that there are no baby lips to kiss.
Their prayers are sighs, their vows most virginal
But a deep need for tenderness and tears.
But why doth Frà Girolamo divert
Her footsteps from the cloister?
Who shall say?
Methinks he favours the Valori's suit,
As I will favour yours.
Well, go and suck
The sweet that waits you.
There are thousand lips
'Twixt Bellosguardo and Fiesole,
Ripening for harvest, that I too might reap,
But keep my sickle for a churlish soil,
And starve amid abundance. Hither come
Del Nero and Ridolfi. They will wean
My pursing lips from bosom that runs dry.

div.stage: [Enter (left) Del Nero and Ridolfi.]

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Tornabuoni. Del Nero. Ridolfi.

lg.l: What tidings from Sarzana?
None as yet.
Save Ludovico's gird when Piero craved
Excuse for having missed him on the road:
“One of us two hath missed his road, 'tis plain,
But 'tis not I, I warrant.”
Much I fear
The gird was true. Purblind in confidence
While the French King yet dallied by the way,
Now that the lazy gonfalons of Charles
Unfurl and flap towards Florence, Piero makes
Obeisance forward.
No worse policy.
How otherwise Lorenzo snatched the State
From imminence of peril, fronting full
A foe declared, yet knitting friends betimes,
Making a turncoat of fixed fate itself,
And outmanœuvring mightiest menaces.
Would he were living now!
Yet we must stand
Fast by the son, that by the father stood.
I never will desert him.
Softly, boy!
Who hinted at desertion? But, if one
You pluck back from a precipice should plunge
Over its edge, would you still follow him?
No; but 'twere well, lest Piero's foot should slip
Through mere mischance, like daring mountaineers
To rope ourselves together.
So we should,
If he in desperate ventures were expert.
But far from risking on the slippery height
Of absolute contention all he hath,
Lo! he goes crawling to the French King's camp,
And seeks his safety in glib lowliness.
Already potent Ottimati, like
Bonsi, Corsini, and Vespucci, join
Their hands with brawling levellers, to run
His pennon from the mast-head of the State.
And have you noted in the public streets
Men of unwonted steadiness of eye,
And handling weapons of another time,
Such as Michele Lando and his band
Of carders brandished ninety years ago
In this same Florence?
Likewise the great Guilds
And Crafts of Industry are all astir,
Foremost among them those of wool and silk.
There's mischief manufacturing.
Sure enough.
And can I cast a ravel in their skein,
Trust me to do it.
You will be well employed;
Better, by far, than lavishing your breath
In the vain chase of a maid's tortuous whims.
The circle of her beauty draws me in.
Then have a care it does not drag you down.
Fie on you, boy! Women should never be
More than the narrow margin of our life,
Past whom its text runs on continuously.
A truth more promptly ta'en to head than heart.
Yet, fervent youth, bear it in memory!
Nor struck there ever timelier hour than this
For purging fancy's sedentary sighs
With draughts of action. Take it from me, boy,
There's no such physic for the love-sick soul
As the brisk air of public policy.
The Signory have summoned in hot haste
This evening a Grand Council. You be there,
As will I and Ridolfi. Fare you well,
Until the Council be convened. How short
Churlish November cuts the genial day!
Under long nights conspiracies can hide.
Be it ours, then, to uncloak them.

div.stage: [Exeunt Del Nero and Ridolfi (left). Enter Candida and Letizia (right). They do not observe Tornabuoni.]

lg.l: Yes, to-night,
After the Council. When the stars are high,
We'll roam together. Mind you fail me not.
There never offered the occasion, sweet,
Of sunning me in your warm gaze, but I
Was quickly perched there. Until then, farewell.

div.stage: [Letizia exit (right). Candida turns to cross the stage; and, after advancing a few steps, sees Tornabuoni, and halts.]

lg.l: Think of the angels! For of you I thought
That very instant! But is instant none
I do not think of you.
Sir, think no more
Of one so little worthy of your thoughts.
'Tis I that am unworthy, well I know,
To house so rich a guest in my poor mind.
But you have entered there and must not quit.
I'll try to furnish it with noble thoughts,
So that you may not feel a stranger in it.
No need to furnish it anew for me.
With nobleness it is already stocked;
And, by that nobleness, I beg you will
Keep it—well, not for me.
If not, for whom?
Surely we are betrothed?
O sir! by whom?
By one who never had the power to bind.
Lorenzo mated us for policy,
I never yielding even mute assent.
Be noble, and forget me!
Hath the will
Power over memory? I shall forget
When all I am pales to oblivion,
But not before.
Then think of me as one
To whom you inclined graciously and got
Best reverence in return. There! let us part.

div.stage: [She is going to pass him, but he bars the way.]

lg.l: Not in this wise, and never in this world,
Unless it be some other have secured
The prize I wrestle for. Tell me out plain:
Is your heart yours to give, or is't enslaved
Unto Valori?
Sir, I think you fail
Somewhat in courtesy. My heart is Heaven's:
No earthly tenant yet hath entered there;
Nor, saving you, hath any sought to force
His way in without knocking.
That is why
They stand without. No chaste maid lifts the latch.
But open it yourself, they lack the strength
To thrust you forth!
Your hand was placed in mine.
Lorenzo plighted us, and that pledge I
Sealed with my melting love, as now I stamp
Myself upon your lips.

div.stage: [He kisses her by force. Enter (right) Savonarola, Frà Domenico, and Frà Silvestro.]

lg.l: Lorenzo Tornabuoni! What is this?
A noble maiden! you, not noble less,
Outrage her modesty!
We are betrothed.
Pardon him, Frà Girolamo, as I,
Freely forgive. But this, in right to me:
If it be true I plighted am to him,
'Twas by Lorenzo, shortly ere he died,
For public ends.
Fie on you, sir, to claim
A bond like that, which Heaven's self hath made void,
Void in its sight before. Go you, my child,
With Frà Silvestro: he will tend you home;
Though I can read in every lineament
You have a guardian angel of your own.

div.stage: [Exeunt (left) Frà Silvestro and Candida. Savonarola and Frà Domenico gaze after them.]

lg.l: Curse on these shaven pates that claim to stand
Betwixt the soul and body! But that kiss
Will sound her soul unto its very depths,
And fetch her up her secret.

div.stage: [Exit (right).]

lg.l: See! he hath gone, nor waited to be chid.
His conscience chides him sharper than can I,
Or he had fled not. Ah! how happy we,
The lawless ardour of whose fleshly lusts
In the cool cloister are extinguishëd.
But we must be indulgent to the heat
Of the unscreened world. I do remember me
How at Ferrara, in my glowing youth,
A daughter of a Florentine exiled
From this contentious city, with a look
Transfixed my heart. She was a Strozzi, but,
She not being born in wedlock, I conceived
His pride might stoop to me, a lowly youth;
But God, who loved me better than all love
Of man or maiden, kept me for His work.
They scorned me,—but enough. Only, my son,
Love, if it happy or unhappy be,
Treat you indulgently.
This maid would wed
The loveless pallet of a convent cell.
I know it; but 'twould be to injure Heaven
Did we the sad and sinking world deprive
Of such sweet household leaven, which should be kept
To make some good man's soul rise higher still,
And lighten his life's heaviness. Come, my son!
We must go pray the Holy Spirit to be
With the Grand Council.

div.stage: [Exeunt (left). Simultaneously enter (right) Salviati, accompanied by a strong band of armed Piagnoni.]

div.head: SCENE III.

lg.l: Take care to stand your ground.
Spini and Soderini and their crew
Of Compagnacci come. But never fear!
The people side with us, and all the Guilds
Have gone against the Medici.

div.stage: [Enter (right) Spini, Soderini, Cei, and the Compagnacci. Then come on the processions of the various Guilds, and occupy the space between the Compagnacci and the Piagnoni. The Signory emerge from the Palazzo Pubblico, with the Dieci de Guerra, the Otto di Balìa, and many leading Citizens, conspicuous among whom are Capponi, Corsini, Bonsi, and Vespucci. They occupy the steps of the Palazzo Pubblico, and the Loggia de' Lanzi. Citizens crowd in where they can.]

lg.l: We are late.
Spread yourselves out.
Remember, not to shout
Till Spini gives the signal.
We shall wait
Vainly for that to-day. 'Tis plain enough
We are outnumbered.
Lord! how dark it grows!
Yes, puzzling dark. We must have torches.
See!
Torches are coming. Friends! make room for them.

div.stage: [Men bearing flaming torches of grease and tow enter.]

lg.l: Silence, good citizens! that you may hear
Proposals from the Signory.
Look! look!
Luca Corsini is about to speak.
He is not the Proposto: Why should he
Break through the law?
Dear fellow-citizens!
I am not the Proposto, neither hath
The Signory invited me to speak.
But times there are when, as the people know,
The people's safety is the highest law.
That's true enough.
And this is one of them.
Charles of Anjou, invited o'er the Alps
By Ludovico Sforza, hath affirmed
His claim to Naples, and with horse and foot,
Frenchmen and Swiss, some fifty thousand strong,
Hath fought his way unto your very doors.
But, fellow-citizens, he doth not come
An enemy to Florence; only asks
A friendly passage.
But our money too.
It seems that Florence always has to pay.
Better to pay in money than in blood,
Which, when 'tis spilt, sucketh up money too.
There, he is right.
Piero de' Medici,
Not heeding this, made of the King a foe.

div.stage: [There is commotion in the Crowd, the Compagnacci crying “No!” but they are shouted down by the Piagnoni, the Guilds, and the People. Corsini grows embarrassed. Young Jacopo de' Nerli rises to back him up.]

lg.l: Yes, made a foe who might have been a friend,
Whereby I tell you—

div.stage: [There is fresh disorder. The father of Jacopo de' Nerli rises.]

lg.l: Pay my son no heed:
He is too young, and of too crude a brain
To give ripe counsel.

div.stage: [Piero Capponi rises.]

lg.l: Let us hear Capponi!
Capponi speaks!

sp.speaker: CAPPONI.

lg.l: Yes, fellow-citizens!
For I have words in me that will not wait,
But claim an exit. Time is it to end
Our childish ways. Piero de' Medici,
Unlike his father, bold yet politic,
Is ruining the Commonwealth. He might,
As you have heard, have bargained with the King,
Who asked nought better. But in lieu of this,
Partly from levity, in part from spite
'Gainst Ludovic of Milan, the King's friend,
He bade the Tuscan fortresses resist
The advance of Charles, who straight laid siege to them.
Know ye the latest tidings? Piero now,
Hastening in terror to the French King's camp,
Hath these your precious strongholds rendered up,
The keys of all our Tuscan territory:
Firstly, Pietrasanta, which to win
Florence a hundred thousand ducats spent;
With it Sarzana, which the State hath cost
Full fifty thousand florins; last of all,
Is Sarzanella.

sp.stage: [There is again commotion in the Crowd, but it is manifest that the preponderance of opinion is against the Medici. Capponi goes on.]

lg.l: Therefore I say once more,
Piero de' Medici is proved unfit
To guide the Commonwealth. Straight let us name
Ambassadors to Charles, who, if they meet
Piero upon the way, salute him not,
But to the King expound from whom it was,
From whom alone, proceeded enmity,
And that in Florence he and the French name
Have ever had and still will find a friend.
Truer he could not speak.
Say, could he?
No!
Long live Capponi!

sp.speaker: CAPPONI.

lg.l: Therefore we must choose
Men of repute and honour to convey
Our welcome to the King. At the same time,
My fellow-citizens, we must not fail
To bring in from the country armèd men,
Trusty of purpose and discreetly led,
Who may within the city's unseen nooks,
Convents and cloisters, snugly be concealed.
And let not any Florentine omit
To have a dagger or a pike at need,
So that if this most Christian King demand
More than a splendid homage at your hands,
With 'chance some solid tribute which the French,
An avaricious race, love best of all,
You then may show him a fixed countenance,
In armour roughly-set.

sp.stage: [The Crowd shout and clash their arms.]

lg.l: And now, my friends,
To choose Ambassadors.
We all choose you!
Good: I will go. But there is one whose name
Is upon every lip, in every heart.
Know you that name?
Yes, Frà Girolamo,
The Prior of Saint Mark!
Ay, none but he,
Savonarola, for he prophesied
The coming of the King across the Alps,
And who alone, nor I nor any one,
But only he, from Florence can avert
The ills invoked by Pier de' Medici.
Wish you that Frà Girolamo should go?
Yes! all—all—all—all of us wish it.

div.stage: [The Compagnacci are cowed and remain silent. Some of them gradually slip away.]

lg.l: To him I your election will convey.
He loves the people and will treat their choice
As though it were a message from on High.
And now, good citizens, disperse; the night
Is deepening fast. Hence to your homes, and trust
The Signory to save the Commonwealth.

div.stage: [The Signory, the Dieci di Guerra, the Otto di Balìa, and leading citizens, retire into the Palazzo Pubblico. The Crowd gradually disperses, the Compagnacci scowling at the Piagnoni, and an air of suspicion and defiance pervading the multitude; but no disturbance takes place. Meanwhile, the following dialogue goes on.]

lg.l: Are you content Savonarola goes
To parley with the King?
Ay, well content.
We all trust Frà Girolamo.
Hence, my friends!
We are outpolled; but should it come to blows,
Sinews will count, not numbers.

div.stage: [Exeunt the rest of the Compagnacci (left), and only Bettuccio and Letizia are left upon the stage.]

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Bettuccio. Letizia.

lg.l: Here she comes,
As punctual as a star and yet more pure.
This is the lady Candida, whom I—
Praising so much, did not yet praise enough.
But I must leave you, momently to hie
To Tornabuoni, and apprise him quick
That matters march awry. 'Twas thought he would
Be present at the Council; but no voice
Could have withstood the torrent of discourse
That foamed 'gainst Piero. Lady, with your leave.

div.stage: [Letizia embraces him. He salutes Candida, and exit (left).]

lg.l: Is that your lover that you told me of?
None else. What think you of him?
He is well,
And deft at courtesy. But have a care
You love not overmuch.
That cannot be.
He is a poet, hence athirst for love,
And one must make a fountain of one's heart,
And keep it flowing.
What if it should well
When he would drink no more?
O, you are wrong,
Echoing a common shout. A poet is
The two extremes of our prosaic mean.
Because he gives so much, much he demands;
No partial love contents him. Being large,
He is not filled with little, but exacts
All that is in this tiny tenement,
And all it vastly longs for.
Happy youth,
To have found one woman in this cautious world
Who keeps back nothing! Heaven scarce were Heaven,
To beggar this so prodigal a heart.
Yet have I heard that love was born a cheat,
And in the end will sweep up all your stakes!
That's when you play with him; a hellish game
No honest woman tries. Bettuccio's long!
I wish he would return.
He scarce has gone.
You think your heart the clock, and that time ticks
With fancy's bounding pulses! How I wish
That your Bettuccio had the grace to choose
A Cause as fair as you. Why does he mate
With Frà Girolamo's worst enemies?
I never questioned him on such a thing,
Since alien 'tis to love. Now, now I must,
Since I perceive that danger lies that way.
This Signor Tornabuoni was the friend
Of his convivial seasons in the days
While yet Lorenzo lived. Men's amity
Is pledged above their beakers; and he vows
That braver gallant never kissed a cup.
He hath a noble port.

div.stage: [Enter Valori (left) breathlessly. Candida plucks at Letizia's gown, to lead her away.]

lg.l: Nay, do not go!
I am in need of some swift messenger.
None is more swift than I will be.
No, no!
You are too dainty for such common work.
Trust me, sir, with your message.
Both can go.
We must not; for Bettuccio would return,
And neither find.
Now, fortune stand by me!
Speed, quick-fledged maiden: I will stand on guard
By this fair lady while your errand runs.
Nor must I quit this place until you bring
Hither the Signory. If in their beds,
Rouse them, and say Valori waits without.
Now quick into the Palace! You must go
Round to the postern entrance.

div.stage: [Exit Letizia (right).]

lg.l: Sir! you seem
To bear grave tidings.
Grave indeed they are,
But graver not to me than news that you
Could give me, an you would.
What may that be?
News, O, so long in coming! Why do you live
Solitary as a swan and as content,
That, on some silent mere sedately moored,
Keeps turning on itself? Yet lone swans have
Somewhere a nest. Oh! make your nest with me,
Deep in the sedges of protecting love,
Where ripples of vexation die away
And winds are barred from coming!
With what ease
You ask what is with difficulty given!
You tell me that you love me. That seems much.
If I love you, I do not know it, sir!
O, why do you delay in loving me?
The fruit that ripens slowly is half sour,
While sweetness comes with quick maturity.
Hush! or you'll wake the night! Look at the stars,
Holding in Heaven their silent colloquy.
Why do they keep so silent?
Is't not because
Silence alone makes perfect harmony,
And in their concord ne'er a false note strikes
To scandalize the ear?
See! One is falling—
Leaving a long trail.
Why doth a shooting star shine brightlier far
Than any that keeps fixëd in its seat?
'Tis, its career, being brief, is glorious.
Who would not into jaws of darkness jump,
Traversing first such bright trajectory?
Hush! Falling stars are high examples sent
To warn, not lure. Gross fancy says they are
Substantial meteors; but that is not so.
They are the merest phantasies of Night,
When she's asleep, and, dimly visited
By past effects, she dreams of Lucifer
Hurled out of Heaven.
How sweetly moralised!
Where did you learn that wisdom?
At my prayers:
A fountain of instruction, much I fear
Men dip into but little. You blasphemed,
So I made solemn your profanity.
Stars are the eyes of night, wherewith she sees
What ill we do, and silence is the ear
With which she listens.
You are too pure a strain
To mix with my impurity.
That proves
You purer than you think. If I could love,
It would be for the strong humility
That bends as low as I am. See, they come.
Now lend your ear unto the State, nor brood
On private yearnings. Florence wants your heart:
Give it her wholly.
At your bidding, yes;
And she, when saved, will give it back to you.

div.stage: [Enter Letizia (right), followed by Corsini, Bonsi, and Vespucci. Candida and Letizia retire.]

lg.l: Forgive me, gentlemen, for treating sleep
As though it were siesta of the day.
But I bear pressing news. All goes amiss.
Come you from Pisa?
Yes, from Pisa straight,
Spurring as fast as hoofs would carry me.
Is the King there?
There, and with all his force
Whither the first Ambassadors we sent,
Unknown to Piero, now have followed him.
But they found Charles at Lucca.
So they did;
And there the King showed reasonable mind.
But Piero, bidding higher, foiled their terms,
And now Charles craftily affects to treat
But with the Medici alone.
Is't true
That Piero hath contracted we shall pay
Two hundred thousand ducats?
So I learned,
Coming along the road. But hear you worse.
Not only Pietrasanta and the twin,
Sarzana, Sarzanella, are unlocked,
But Piero hath engaged to render up
Pisa.
What! Pisa!
Yes, and with them too
Leghorn and Ripafratta.
News the ear
Can scarce think audible.
And ne'er a tongue,
Unless it were Valori's, could announce,
And be believed.
Alas! 'tis positive!
And with it snaps the ultimate frail link
That tied me to the Medici.
Yet stay!
What if against the city Charles advance,
Conveying Piero with him?
Never fear!
Fool though he be, he hath the wit to know
That if into the saddle tilted back
By Charles or any other, Florence quick,
When these had gone, would buck him out of it.
He needs must grasp the stirrup for himself,
Or never mount again.
He clutches now.
For the boy Cardinal who should have worn
The plain male garb of statecraft, and have left
The sacristy's adornments epicene
Unto this Piero, in his brother's cause
Works day and night through all the thoroughfares,
Lavishing gold, and plying still the cry
Of Palle! Palle! but no echo finds.

div.stage: [Enter (left) Marcuccio Salviati in hot haste.]

lg.l: No palliation, gentlemen, I plead,
For breaking on your conference. The news
I bring is my excuse. Not one chime since,
Paolo Orsini, coming from without,
Seized on San Gallo Gate, and occupies
That quarter wholly.
Does he come in strength?
Five hundred horse and twice as many foot,
And all the rabble shout for the Medici.
That is the slum where still the vermin hide.
But 'tis believed Piero himself hath set
His face towards the city.
May it be true!
See, Salviati, that your trustiest hands
For no excuse disperse, and keep them near!
Apprise the Guilds. I will not fail to lend
Assistance opportune. The Signory
Will do the rest.

div.stage: Salviati retires (left).]

lg.l: 'Tis patent, peril lurks
In this advancëd night, and will unfold
Its tokens with the dawn. Who is't to-day
Is the Proposto?
Intempestively,
Antonio Lorini, who commands
Likewise the Palace Keys; so we took care
He was not woke.
As care too will we take
Out of his hand betimes the keys shall slip,
Should they be wanted.
Let us to our posts,
And sleep no more! The night now nears its term,
And from its womb will issue forth a day
With freedom's chrism fair Florence shall baptize.
Valori! be familiar with your sword!

div.stage: [He draws his sword, and kisses the blade, then salutes the three, and they all retire.]

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: [Various signs of early morning. People living in the houses in the Piazza open their windows, throw back the persiane, and look out. Artisans pass across the square. Women come to the fountain with pitchers and brazen vessels. Enter (left) Spini, Soderini, and Cei.]

lg.l: San Gallo Gate is safely held, and there
Piero will find an entrance.
As a rat
Doth to a trap that is to throttle him.
Think you that, Soderini?
Faith! I do.
All the Guilds go against us. If it were
Only the Piagnoni showed their teeth,
Well, they might snarl; but folk that know to bite
Have begun barking.
Is it true the arms
In the Bargello have been seized upon?
There's not a brat but brandishes a blade,
And blusters for the People.
Look! they stream
From every street and passage hitherward,
Clumsy with weapons. We had best retire,
And keep our folk in hand.

div.stage: [Exeunt (right). People come trooping into the Piazza from all sides, armed with rusty swords, broken rapiers, old-fashioned pikes, etc.]

lg.l: No work to-day, I warrant.
Deuce a stroke.
I've shut up shop.
We're all for Liberty.
Fine folks may wait for once: needle and awl
Must have a holiday.
They will be fortunate
If they get shaved.
They're pretty sure of that.
Your barber is in wrangling times of peace
A valiant politician; but the edge
Of his sharp wit grows blunt when risk's to shear.
Ay, ay, your tailor is the likeliest man,
When clothes are to be torn.
Save cobblers, who
Are useful when you want to run away,
And not to slip.

div.stage: [The Crowd laugh. Suddenly a noise is heard in the distance, and all of them rush towards the back of the stage, to see whence it proceeds. They give way as the sound gets nearer, and retire towards each side of the stage.]

lg.l: It's Pier' de' Medici.
Hath he returned?
Look if he hasn't! with courtiers at his heels,
But courtiers with their forks out.

div.stage: [Enter Piero, attended by his brother the Cardinal, Paolo Orsini, and a goodly following of armed men.]

lg.l: Have you not got a cheer? Hath garlic ta'en
The sweetness from your breath?
Down with the Medici!
We want no Medici!
Want, or not want,
You'll have to bolt them.

div.stage: [Orsini and his followers drive the people back, and overawe them. Piero walks to the main door of the Palazzo Pubblico, and ascends the steps. As he does so the doors are thrown open, and the Signory, headed by Corsini, Bonsi, and Vespucci, appear in the doorway.]

lg.l: Piero de' Medici, what want you here?
To enter as I entered have before,
Whene'er I willed.
Your will no more is law.
You to King Charles would sell the Commonwealth
That is not to be bartered.
Leave, I say!
Pass through I will.
Then through the postern gate,
Where others pass.

div.stage: [The Cardinal and Orsini rush forward to abet Piero, but they are too late. The doors are shut in Piero's face. The Crowd take courage, and begin to hiss. Piero draws his sword, as though he would use violence against them. At that moment the bell of the Tower of the Palazzo Pubblico begins to sound. Fresh Crowds hurry into the Piazza, where reigns the utmost confusion, the people crying, “Popolo e Libertà!” “Abbasso le Palle!” In the confusion, Piero, still with sword drawn, retires, covered by Orsini, the Cardinal, and their followers. Tornabuoni, Ridolfi, and Del Nero enter, followed by Spini and the Compagnacci, who shout, “Palle! Palle!” “Long live the Medici!” But Valori, with an armed retinue, appears, and the party of the Medici gradually retire, till the stage is occupied only by the Piagnoni and the People, who shout, “Popolo e Libertà!” Tornabuoni, Del Nero, and Ridolfi linger; and a Crier appears on the steps of the Palazzo Pubblico.]

lg.l: Five thousand florins will be paid to him
Who Pier' de' Medici brings here alive,
Or Cardinal Giovanni; and, if dead,
Two thousand florins. This the Signory
Promises solemnly, and thus proclaims
Both rebels and both outlaws.

div.stage: [Enter Salviati.]

lg.l: An offer made too late. Pier' de' Medici
Passed through San Gallo Gate, and spurs him fast
On to Bologna, in the company
Of his brother Giuliano.
Libertà!
Popolo e Libertà. Down with the Medici!
Hence to the Podestà, and drag we down
The effigies placed there by Cosimo
In '34; and with them those that look
From the Dogana gate, more recent trace
Of rule to be obliterated now!

div.stage: [Exeunt Valori and his retinue, followed by the People.]

lg.l: How light these new keels run before the wind!
Let us but help them with a following breath,
They will capsize.
I rather would confront
Their giddy course and send them staggering down,
Than lead them forward.
You were best in port
Until this hurricane shall cease to blow.
Follow an old man's counsel, and depart.
That, if I must. But never will I catch
A watchword from their greasy mouths and smack
My lips upon it; so, for now, farewell!

div.stage: [Exit Tornabuoni (right). Enter Salviati (left)].

lg.l: Sir, you had best go crouch. The people gut
Your son Antonio's hearth; the like they do
To Giovanni Guidi, and no less
To Antonio Miniati. Passing on
From Via Larga, where they sacked the house
Of the young Cardinal, they plunder now
His treasures in the garden of Saint Mark.
Your turn will surely come.
Then let us hide,
While yet is time.

div.stage: [Del Nero and Ridolfi prepare to depart; but the populace enter again from different points, crying “Abbasso le palle!” Del Nero and Ridolfi shout “Popolo e Libertà!”]

lg.l: Ha! here they are! And harken how they shout
For Freedom, as the devil brought to bay
Mouths Scripture.
Let us make an end of them!
They are enemies to the people.
No, not death,
But only fire. Hence let us to their homes!
Yes, yes! We'll teach these lords of privilege
What freedom means!

div.stage: [Savonarola, attended by FràDomenico, Frà Silvestro, and other Monks, suddenly appears on the Piazza.]

div.head: SCENE VI.

lg.l: Hold! Christians! Florentines!
What wickedness is this? Hath the Lord God
Delivered you from tyranny of One,
Only to let this city undergo
The tyranny of Many? Truce henceforth,
Truce to vindictiveness! God spares who could
Crush all His enemies; you too must spare.
The Medici have gone, have fallen, have fled,
And all the meretricious gauds of power
Have brushed your Gates. Down on your knees and give
Thanksgiving unto Christ who liberates,
And liberated you. The French King comes;
And how will you receive him if your hands
Be black with burning Christian hearths? Forbear,
As ye would be forborne with. Know, the Scourge
Hath not yet passed. The Sword of the Lord still hangs
Aloft in the sky. Would ye avert it, show
Mercy to the unmerciful. No more blood,
And no more fire, but prayer, and love, and peace.
Shortly you will be summoned to pronounce
On your new Government; but no more blood for fire,
Nor ransacking of roofs! Florence is free,
And Christ is King! Clamour ye loud for Christ.
Now and henceforth King of the Commonwealth!
Long live Christ! Long live the Commonwealth!
Long live Savonarola!
Now await
The entry of King Charles with mingled mien
Of Christians and of freemen. As a friend
He comes; a friendly welcome lend to him.
The Scourge of the new Cyrus shall descend
On other walls than yours, if carnal toys
You put away, and mortify the flesh,
Indulged so long. Now once more, Long live Christ!

div.stage: [The People again shout as Savonarola bids them, and gradually disperse. He too retires, followed by his Monks. Enter Grosso (right), followed by his Wife.]

lg.l: Rate me no more. The artist's mind should brood
On its intention long and silently;
But you so often lift me from the nest,
My purpose cools, and that which might have been
Matured to punctual perfectness, when hatched
Is part abortive.
Keep your simile,
To mend yourself. You never are on cluck,
Unless the fair Letizia be at hand
To clap you to a sitting. Why should she
Be indispensable the more than I?
My bust is shapelier far than hers, my arm
More ripe and rounded. She is raw and lean.
Her daintiest charms are locked against your gaze,
At least they ought to be, and shall be, too,
Whilst mine are at your bidding.
True, good wife.
But Art is less material than you deem,
And gloats on the invisible. Besides,
This maiden sits so patiently, she lends
A sympathetic instinct to my touch.
She never rails at me, but smiles as sweet
As fresh-culled spray of dewy eglantine,
Whose blossom, pinky-white, is half unclosed,
Half shut upon itself.
She flatters you,
Plain with her tongue, yet plainer with her eye;
And men with adulation can be caught
As easily as flies with syrup are.
Thicker and coarser that the mixture be,
The more they stick.
Then why not try that way,
To hold me fast? My duty is to you,
Likewise my wont. But never doubt of this:
My fancy wanders unrestrainedly,
Alighting upon all things fair and sweet,
And with what sugared bounty they secrete
Stocking invention's hive, that cannot live
On one sole flower, howe'er with honey brimmed.
If this be infidelity, I am
The most unfaithful vagabond alive;
And so rail on.

div.stage: [Exit Anita, in dudgeon (left). Enter Salviati and Piagnoni (right).]

lg.l: Come on, my fellows, we are here in time
To pick the choicest standing-ground, nor lose
One word of wisdom by our elders dropped.
There! Range you so! Ho, Grosso! Is it you?
Have you, too, come to hear the tough debate
Between the Frenchmen and our Signory?
Not I, in sooth. There's talk enough at home
Without resorting to the market-place.
Argue away; I will retire me where
Time is not squandered in vain controversy,
But what I think, I do.
That gentleman
Thinks not thin wine of himself.
Which of them does?
These transcendental artists in the end
Idealize themselves.
I often thank God
I was not born a sculptor.
Nor a poet.
They are worst of all.

div.stage: [Enter Spini and Soderini (right).]

lg.l: A merry time you'll have,
Now that the Medici have gone. The French
Are chalking all your doors.
What! Have they come?
Thick through San Frediano Gate they stream
And eddy where they will.
I think I had best
Go home and see what's doing.
Better not:
